newsitem.title: UK: Ministers curb early British election speculation.
newsitem.headline: Ministers curb early British election speculation.

text.p: Two senior cabinet ministers moved on Friday to dampen fevered media speculation about an early British election by insisting that Prime Minister John Major wanted to delay a poll for another 3-1/2 months.
Defence Secretary Michael Portillo said May 1 was the date Major preferred, while Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said he saw no reason why the government could not carry on until then.
The death on Thursday of Conservative legislator Iain Mills pushed the government into a minority in parliament, with 323 opposition MPs facing 322 of Major's supporters.
A minority government has not been seen in Britain since 1979, and the new situation provoked immediate discussion in the media of whether Major could hang on in power.
The pro-Conservative Daily Telegraph newspaper said some senior party members were pressing Major for a quick contest and were preparing for a poll as early as March 20.

It noted that the Conservatives had brought forward a conference of their Welsh party to February 14, booked large numbers of advertising hoardings for March and April and scheduled two nationwide TV broadcasts for the next four weeks.
But Portillo, questioned by reporters during a visit to Renfrew, Scotland, said: "John Major has suggested that May 1 may be his preferred date. That seems fine to me."
And Heseltine, speaking in Bolton, northern England, said: "The Prime Minister has indicated a preference for going full time, and we can't see any reason why we shouldn't do that."
May 22 is technically the last possible date for an election, but May 1 -- the same date as local elections -- is widely seen as the last feasible one.

Heseltine said that despite the government's apparently parlous parliamentary position, it was winning most votes by a clear margin, and it wanted to enact its legislative programme before going to the country.
An opinion poll in the Telegraph on Friday showed the Conservatives 18 percentage points behind the opposition Labour Party, but suggested the gap had closed in the last month.

Major, whose party has suffered from a civil war over European policy and from a series of financial and sexual scandals involving its MPs, is hoping that an improving British economy will boost its standing in the polls by May.
Despite Portillo's and Heseltine's remarks, pre-election campaigning continued apace on Friday.
Interior minister Michael Howard told businessmen in Birmingham Labour would weaken British industry by importing protective labour regulations from the European continent.
"It wouldn't be long before once again we read the headlines we have always read whenever there's been a Labour government, the headlines which read "Unemployment up Again'," he said.
Labour's Trade and Industry spokeswoman Margaret Beckett hit back by repeating her party's claims that a new Conservative government would put value added tax on food.
"The Tories are addicted to VAT. They can't break the habit, but like all addicts, they lie and claim they have," she told constituents in Derby, central England.
